section.title: Manna and Quail
section.sectionRationale: Hunger, not thirst, is the next test of the wilderness, and God answers it with a daily miracle that teaches Israel dependence, obedience, and the meaning of the Sabbath rest, all at once. Jesus later takes up this very chapter to explain who He is.
section.thesis: When Israel grumbles for food, the LORD rains down bread from heaven and sends quail, testing whether His people will gather only what they need, trust Him for the seventh day without gathering, and remember, for every generation to come, the bread He gave them in the wilderness.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Israel's grumbling for the food of Egypt; God's promise of bread and meat and the reason for it; the manna and quail actually given, gathered, and mismanaged; the Sabbath test of trust; and the jar of manna kept as a lasting memorial.

units.label: Grumbling in the desert
units.note: we sat by pots of meat

verses.text: On the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left the land of Egypt, the whole congregation of Israel set out from Elim and came to the Desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai.
And there in the desert they all grumbled against Moses and Aaron.

“If only we had died by the LORD's hand in the land of Egypt!” they said. “There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread, but you have brought us into this desert to starve this whole assembly to death!”

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions.
Then on the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather on the other days.”
So Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, “This evening you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,
and in the morning you will see the LORD's glory, because He has heard your grumbling against Him. For who are we that you should grumble against us?”

And Moses added, “The LORD will give you meat to eat this evening and bread to fill you in the morning, for He has heard your grumbling against Him. Who are we? Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD.”
Then Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the whole congregation of Israel, ‘Come before the LORD, for He has heard your grumbling.’”
And as Aaron was speaking to the whole congregation of Israel, they looked toward the desert, and there in a cloud the glory of the LORD appeared.
Then the LORD said to Moses,
“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, ‘At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.’”

units.label: Manna and quail given
units.note: what is it? and gathering according to need

media.alt: Thin flakes on the desert floor at dawn
media.caption: Bread from heaven, given fresh every morning.

verses.text: That evening quail came and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp.
When the layer of dew had evaporated, there were thin flakes on the desert floor, as fine as frost on the ground.

When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. 
So Moses told them, “It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.
This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Each one is to gather as much as he needs. You may take an {{omer|omer}} for each person in your tent.’”
So the Israelites did this. Some gathered more, and some less.
When they measured it by the omer, he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall. Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat.
Then Moses said to them, “No one may keep any of it until morning.”
But they did not listen to Moses; some people left part of it until morning, and it became infested with maggots and began to smell. So Moses was angry with them.
Every morning each one gathered as much as was needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.

units.label: The Sabbath rest
units.note: a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath

verses.text: On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much food, two omers per person, and all the leaders of the congregation came and reported this to Moses.

He told them, “This is what the LORD has said: ‘Tomorrow is to be a day of complete rest, a holy {{sabbath|Sabbath}} to the LORD. So bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil. Then set aside whatever remains and keep it until morning.’”
So they set it aside until morning as Moses had commanded, and it did not smell or contain any maggots.
“Eat it today,” Moses said, “because today is a Sabbath to the LORD. Today you will not find anything in the field.
For six days you may gather, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, it will not be there.”
Yet on the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they did not find anything.
Then the LORD said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions?
Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day He will give you bread for two days. On the seventh day, everyone must stay where he is; no one may leave his place.”
So the people rested on the seventh day.
Now the house of Israel called the bread manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey.

Moses said, “This is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’”
So Moses told Aaron, “Take a jar and fill it with an omer of manna. Then place it before the LORD to be preserved for the generations to come.”
And Aaron placed it in front of the Testimony, to be preserved just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
The Israelites ate manna forty years, until they came to a land where they could settle; they ate manna until they reached the border of Canaan.
(Now an omer is a tenth of an ephah.)

omer.gloss: A dry measure, roughly two liters, a tenth of an ephah. God commanded each person to gather exactly one omer, no more, no less, a built-in check on hoarding and a daily lesson in trusting Him for enough.

sabbath.gloss: Rest, cessation from labor. Introduced here even before the Sinai commandments, the Sabbath is tied directly to trusting God's provision, since no manna fell on the seventh day and yet the sixth day's gathering never spoiled.

basic.context: Six weeks after leaving Egypt, Israel runs out of food and grumbles that they were better off as slaves. God responds by raining down bread every morning and sending quail every evening, but He also builds in a daily test: gather only what you need, and trust Him enough to rest on the seventh day.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, sustained forty-year provision for a real people in the wilderness. It is not primarily about food but about trust: whether Israel would obey God's instructions about gathering, hoarding, and resting, even when it seemed to make no practical sense.
basic.originalLanguages: Each person was to gather exactly one omer, a fixed measure that left no room for either shortage or greedy excess. The whole test turns on the shabbat, the rest, that God commanded on the seventh day, built into the very rhythm of daily bread long before it becomes a formal commandment at Sinai.
basic.typology: This bread from heaven, given daily and insufficient to hoard, anticipates Jesus' own description of Himself in John 6 as the true bread from heaven, given not just for a day but for eternal life, and His teaching His disciples to pray for daily bread.
basic.christ: In John 6:32-35, Jesus explicitly points back to this chapter and declares that He, not the manna, is the true bread from heaven, giving life to the world; whoever comes to Him will never hunger, fulfilling and surpassing what manna could only picture for a season.
basic.god: God hears grumbling and responds with generous provision rather than punishment, yet He also insists on obedience in how that provision is received, testing whether His people will trust Him daily rather than hoard for tomorrow. His care and His holiness are not in tension; both are expressed in the same provision.
basic.crossReferences: John 6:31-35 has Jesus identify Himself as the true bread from heaven that this manna foreshadowed. Hebrews 9:4 notes the golden jar of manna kept in the ark as a lasting testimony. Matthew 6:11 echoes this chapter's rhythm of daily bread in the Lord's Prayer.
basic.oneStory: God feeds a grumbling, undeserving people daily, testing whether they will trust Him rather than hoard or grasp for control. That pattern of daily, dependent trust in God's provision runs through the whole Bible and finds its true fulfillment in Christ, the bread from heaven who satisfies forever.

context.literary:
Exodus 16 is the longest of the wilderness episodes before Sinai, and its length is part of its message. Marah took six verses; the manna takes thirty six, because it is not a single rescue but a daily pattern that must be learned. The chapter is built around repeated instructions and repeated failures. God tells them to gather each day, verse 4; they are told to leave nothing until morning, and some do, verse 20; they are told nothing will be found on the seventh day, and some go out anyway, verse 27. Each failure is followed by a word from Moses or the LORD, and the chapter ends with the people finally resting, verse 30.

The word 'grumbling' is its hinge. It appears again and again in verses 2 to 12, and Moses first asks, 'who are we that you should grumble against us?' verse 7, then insists, 'Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD,' verse 8. The same section repeats the phrase that God 'has heard' it, verses 7, 8, 9 and 12. The complaint is loud, but the reader is told that God is listening.

The promises are paired: in the evening they will know that the LORD brought them out of Egypt, and in the morning they will see His glory, verses 6 and 7; at twilight meat, in the morning bread, verse 12. That evening and morning rhythm recalls the refrain of Genesis 1, and the chapter moves toward a seventh day of rest just as the creation account does.

The closing verses, 31 to 36, step outside the story. They describe the manna, record the jar kept 'before the Testimony,' and note that Israel ate it for forty years until they reached Canaan. The Testimony, the tablets of the covenant, has not yet been given, and the forty years have not yet passed. The narrator looks ahead from the first morning of manna to its last, framing the whole wilderness journey as one long lesson in daily dependence.
context.historical:
The date in verse 1, the fifteenth day of the second month, places the scene exactly one month after the exodus, which began on the fifteenth day of the first month, Numbers 33:3. The Desert of Sin, whose name the BSB footnote links with Sinai, lies between Elim and the mountain. A month of travel had used up whatever food the people had carried out of Egypt, and a crowd of that size with its herds would have found almost nothing to eat in the desert.

Their memory of Egypt had already been rewritten. They speak of sitting by pots of meat and eating their fill of bread, verse 3, though the same people had cried out under forced labour, Exodus 2:23. The wish 'If only we had died by the LORD's hand in the land of Egypt' treats the plagues on Egypt as a better fate than God's leading.

Quail migrate across the Sinai peninsula in large numbers in spring and autumn, often flying low and landing exhausted, and the timing here, in the spring after Passover, fits that pattern. Numbers 11:31 attributes a later quail fall to a wind sent by the LORD. The manna has been compared with sweet, sticky deposits found on tamarisk shrubs in the region, which the local people have long gathered. But the text describes something no natural product explains: enough every day for the whole nation, a double portion on the sixth day, nothing on the seventh, food that rotted overnight on ordinary days but kept over the Sabbath, and a supply that ceased the day after they ate the produce of Canaan, Joshua 5:12.

The omer was a household dry measure, about two litres, and the note in verse 36 that it is a tenth of an ephah suggests the measure was no longer familiar to later readers. The jar placed 'before the Testimony' was later understood to have been kept in the ark itself, Hebrews 9:4.
context.canonical:
The manna becomes one of the Old Testament's great memories of grace. Moses interprets it in Deuteronomy 8:3: God fed them with manna 'so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.' Deuteronomy 8:16 adds that it was given 'to humble you and test you, so that in the end He might cause you to prosper.' Nehemiah's prayer recalls that God 'did not withhold Your manna from their mouths' even after the golden calf, Nehemiah 9:20.

The Psalms tell the story two ways. Psalm 105:40 celebrates it: 'They asked, and He brought quail and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.' Psalm 78 tells it as a warning. The people 'willfully tested God by demanding the food they craved,' Psalm 78:18, and though 'He rained down manna for them to eat... Man ate the bread of angels,' Psalm 78:24-25, His anger came on them, drawing on the later quail episode of Numbers 11.

That later episode is the darker twin of Exodus 16. After Sinai the people despise the manna, 'there is nothing to see but this manna!' Numbers 11:6, and the quail they crave become a plague, so that the place is named Kibroth-hattaavah, the graves of craving, Numbers 11:34.

The New Testament uses the chapter in three ways. Paul quotes verse 18 to urge generosity between churches, 'He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall,' 2 Corinthians 8:15. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy's lesson from the manna when He is tempted, Matthew 4:4, and in John 6, after feeding a crowd in the wilderness, He calls Himself 'the bread of life' and 'the living bread that came down from heaven,' John 6:35 and 6:51. Finally, Hebrews 9:4 remembers the gold jar of manna in the ark, and the risen Christ promises 'the hidden manna' to the one who overcomes, Revelation 2:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to learn that their life depended on the LORD every single day. Egypt had fed them in slavery; God would feed them in freedom, but in a way that kept them close to Him. Bread that could not be stored meant trust that could not be stored either. Each morning they had to believe again that He would provide.

He also wanted them to learn to listen. God says plainly that the manna is a test, 'whether or not they will follow My instructions,' verse 4, and the chapter records who listened and who did not. The problem exposed is not ignorance but refusal: 'How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions?' verse 28.

He wanted them to receive the Sabbath as a gift before they received it as a law. 'Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath,' verse 29. Rest came before Sinai, woven into the pattern of God's provision, so that Israel would learn that ceasing from work is an act of trust in the God who provides.

Finally, he wanted every later generation to remember. The jar of manna was kept 'so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness,' verse 32. Israel in the land, with fields and harvests, would be tempted to forget that its bread still came from God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The manna itself was a unique provision for one people in one wilderness, and it ceased when they entered Canaan, Joshua 5:12. The passage does not promise that God will feed believers by miracle today, nor does it command a specific method of gathering food.

Some parts do carry forward, each through the rest of Scripture. The lesson of daily dependence is taught by Jesus in the prayer 'Give us each day our daily bread,' Luke 11:3, and in His warning, 'do not worry about tomorrow,' Matthew 6:34. The principle that no one should have excess while another has shortfall is applied by Paul to Christian giving, 2 Corinthians 8:13-15. The Sabbath command becomes part of the Ten Commandments, Exodus 20:8-11. Christians differ on how that command applies now, but the New Testament affirms that it was 'made for man,' Mark 2:27, and that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:9.

The grumbling, the hoarding and the Sabbath gathering are recorded as warnings, not models, and Paul makes that use of them explicit in 1 Corinthians 10:10-11.

debates.question: Why does the Sabbath appear here, before the Ten Commandments are given at Sinai?

views.label: A creation ordinance made explicit
views.case: God rested on the seventh day and 'blessed the seventh day and sanctified it,' Genesis 2:3, and the fourth commandment grounds itself in creation, Exodus 20:11. On this view the Sabbath was built into the created order, and Exodus 16 is where Israel is first told to keep it.

views.label: A new gift to Israel
views.case: Genesis never records anyone keeping the seventh day, and verse 29 says 'the LORD has given you the Sabbath,' as if it were new. Later it is called a sign 'between Me and you for the generations to come,' Exodus 31:13, pointing to its role as a covenant sign given to Israel.

debates.bearing: Both views see the Sabbath tied to trust in God's provision rather than to human effort. The manna shows the rest as something received, and the New Testament presents its fulfilment as a rest entered by faith in Christ, Hebrews 4:9-10.

debates.question: Was the manna a natural substance or wholly miraculous?

views.label: A natural substance multiplied and timed by God
views.case: Some note the resemblance between manna and sweet deposits found on desert shrubs, which melt in the heat and are still gathered in the region. On this view God used a natural provision, but in amounts and on a schedule only He could arrange.

views.label: A unique miracle
views.case: Others point out that the text stresses what no natural substance could do: feed a nation daily for forty years, double on the sixth day, fail on the seventh, spoil overnight except on the Sabbath, and stop the day after they ate Canaan's crops, Joshua 5:12. Deuteronomy 8:3 calls it food 'which neither you nor your fathers had known.'

debates.bearing: Whatever the physical nature of the manna, Scripture presents it as a direct gift from God, 'the bread that the LORD has given you to eat,' verse 15. Its timing, measure and pattern are what make it a lesson in trust.

study.originalLanguages:
The name manna comes from the people's first question. When they saw it they asked, man hu, 'What is it?' verse 15, and the BSB footnote on verse 31 notes that 'manna' sounds like that Hebrew question. The bread of heaven was named by a confession of ignorance. It was food 'which neither you nor your fathers had known,' Deuteronomy 8:3.

The LORD says He will 'rain down' bread from heaven, verse 4. The verb is matar in its causative form, used of God sending rain, and earlier of the LORD who 'rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah,' Genesis 19:24, and of the hail on Egypt, Exodus 9:23. The same heaven that rained judgment on Egypt now rains bread on Israel. Psalm 78:24 picks up the verb, 'He rained down manna for them to eat,' and John 6:31 quotes the next line, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'

The evening meat comes 'at twilight,' literally 'between the two evenings,' as the BSB footnote on verse 12 explains. It is the same expression used for the slaughter of the Passover lamb, Exodus 12:6. The first meal God gives in the desert is timed like the Passover meal.

The word 'glory' in verses 7 and 10 is kavod, whose root means heaviness or weight, and so honour and splendour. The same root was used when God said He would 'gain honor' through Pharaoh at the sea, Exodus 14:4 and 14:17. Here the glory is seen in the cloud facing the desert, a preview of the glory that will fill the tabernacle, Exodus 40:34.

Each person was to gather 'as much as he needs,' verse 16, literally 'according to his eating.' The phrase recurs in verses 18 and 21, making the point three times: the measure was need, not greed.

When the hoarded manna 'began to smell,' verse 20, the verb is baash, to stink. It was used of the Nile after the first plague, 'the river will stink,' Exodus 7:18, and of the heaps of dead frogs, Exodus 8:14, and the foremen had used it to tell Moses, 'you have made us a stench before Pharaoh,' Exodus 5:21. Hoarding God's gift puts the stench of Egypt back into Israel's tents.

Verse 23 is the first place in the Bible where the noun shabbat, 'Sabbath,' occurs. Genesis 2:2-3 uses the related verb, God 'rested.' Here it is joined to shabbaton, 'a day of complete rest,' a heightened form that later describes the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 23:3 and 16:31. Finally, the 'jar' of verse 33 is a rare word, and the Greek Old Testament described it as a golden jar, which is how Hebrews 9:4 remembers it: 'the gold jar of manna.'

typology.fulfillment: God rained bread from heaven for a hungry people who could not feed themselves. Jesus says, 'it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven,' John 6:32, and then, 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35. The escalation is sharp: 'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died,' John 6:49, but 'the one who eats this bread will live forever,' John 6:58. The manna sustained bodies for a day; Christ gives His flesh 'for the life of the world,' John 6:51.

typology.type: The Sabbath rest given with the manna, Exodus 16:29-30
typology.fulfillment: On the seventh day Israel stopped gathering and lived on what God had already given. Hebrews builds on Israel's wilderness story to say that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' and that 'whoever enters God's rest also rests from his own work,' Hebrews 4:9-10. In Christ believers cease from trying to provide their own righteousness and rest in what He has finished. Israel's weekly rest was a sign that pointed ahead; the rest of Hebrews 4 is the reality, still to be fully entered.

typology.type: The jar of manna kept before the LORD, Exodus 16:33
typology.fulfillment: A portion of manna was kept in the sanctuary as a witness to God's provision, later kept in the ark, Hebrews 9:4. To the one who overcomes the risen Christ promises 'the hidden manna,' Revelation 2:17, food kept in God's presence for His people. The jar held a memory of past provision; the hidden manna is a promise of future provision that never spoils. What was preserved behind the veil for Israel to remember is given openly to believers to enjoy.

typology.type: Equal portions gathered by all, Exodus 16:18
typology.fulfillment: Whoever gathered much had no excess and whoever gathered little had no shortfall. Paul applies the verse to the churches, urging the Corinthians to share their surplus with the poor in Jerusalem 'so that there may be equality,' 2 Corinthians 8:13-15. In Christ, the one who 'became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, God's people share His provision with each other. The wilderness equality was enforced by the manna itself; in the church it is expressed through willing generosity.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly because Jesus Himself takes it up. In John 6 He has just fed five thousand in a remote place, and the crowd asks for a sign, reminding Him that 'Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness,' John 6:31. Jesus corrects them on two counts. It was not Moses but His Father who gave the bread, and the manna was not the true bread. 'The bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world,' John 6:33. Then He says plainly, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger,' John 6:35.

The details of Exodus 16 sharpen the claim. Israel asked 'What is it?' of the manna; the crowd in John 6 asks, in effect, who is this, since 'Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph?' John 6:42. And the crowd in John 6 does what their fathers did: 'the Jews began to grumble about Jesus because He had said, I am the bread that came down from heaven,' John 6:41. The manna was given in response to grumbling; the true bread is met with grumbling too.

Jesus goes further than the manna in every direction. The manna lasted a day; He gives eternal life, John 6:58. The manna fed Israel; He gives His flesh 'for the life of the world,' John 6:51. The manna came down on the dew; He came down from heaven as a person. And the manna ceased at the border of Canaan, but the bread of life sustains His people all the way into the kingdom.

The chapter also points to Christ by His own wilderness. When He was hungry after forty days, the tempter urged Him to make bread from stones. Jesus answered with the lesson Moses drew from the manna: 'Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God,' Matthew 4:4. Israel grumbled for bread; Jesus trusted His Father's word.

Finally, the chapter's lessons are taken into Christian life by Christ's teaching. He taught His disciples to pray 'Give us each day our daily bread,' Luke 11:3, and not to worry about tomorrow, Matthew 6:34. And at His table He gives bread that proclaims His death until He comes, 1 Corinthians 11:26. The daily bread of the wilderness becomes a daily trust in the Father who gave His Son.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He hears. The people grumble against Moses and Aaron, but four times the text says the LORD 'has heard' their grumbling, verses 7, 8, 9 and 12. He is not deaf to complaint, even unfair complaint. And His response is not what they deserved. He does not destroy them; He feeds them.

He reveals Himself through His gifts. The meat in the evening would show 'that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' verse 6, and the bread in the morning would reveal His glory, verse 7. The goal is stated in verse 12: 'Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.' God's gifts are not only for survival but for knowledge of Him. He wants a people who know who is feeding them.

He tests to train. 'In this way I will test whether or not they will follow My instructions,' verse 4. The test is not a trap. It is the daily practice of trusting His word enough to leave nothing for tomorrow and to rest when He says rest.

He is precise and fair in His giving. Each person received what he needed; the one who gathered more had no excess and the one who gathered less had no lack, verse 18. God's provision is not a scramble in which the strong win. And He is generous enough to provide ahead of time: bread for two days on the sixth day, so that His people could rest on the seventh, verse 29.

He is holy, and His holiness shapes time. The seventh day is 'a holy Sabbath to the LORD,' verse 23. God sets apart a day for Himself, and in doing so He gives it to His people as rest. His holiness here is not a burden but a gift.

He is patient and persistent. When some disobeyed and kept manna until morning, it rotted. When some went out on the Sabbath, they found nothing. God allowed the consequences to teach, and asked, 'How long will you refuse?' verse 28, but He still sent the manna the next morning, and for forty years, verse 35.

For worship, the chapter calls us to see our daily bread as God's gift, to give thanks for it, to trust Him for tomorrow, and to rest in Him. The God who fed Israel is the Father who knows what we need before we ask, Matthew 6:8.

crossReferences.note: Israel set out from Rameses 'on the fifteenth day of the first month.' Exodus 16:1 dates the arrival in the Desert of Sin to the fifteenth day of the second month, exactly one month later. The grumbling for food comes a month into freedom, when supplies from Egypt had run out.

Moses explains the manna forty years later: God humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with food they had not known, so that they would understand that 'man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.' The daily test of Exodus 16:4 was training in trusting God's word.

The post-Sinai version of this chapter. The people despise the manna and crave meat, and when quail come, the LORD strikes them with a plague. Where Exodus 16 shows God's patience before the covenant, Numbers 11 shows the seriousness of ingratitude after it.

The psalmist retells the manna as an act of grace to a people who tested God: 'He rained down manna for them to eat; He gave them grain from heaven. Man ate the bread of angels.' It supplies the words the crowd quotes to Jesus in John 6:31.

The manna ceased the day after Israel ate from the produce of Canaan. The note in Exodus 16:35 that they ate it forty years until they reached the land is fulfilled exactly. God's miraculous provision ended when His ordinary provision through the land began.

Paul quotes Exodus 16:18, 'He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall,' to urge the Corinthians to share their surplus with needy believers. The equality God enforced in the wilderness is to be practised freely in the church.

Hungry in the wilderness after forty days, Jesus refuses to make bread for Himself and answers the tempter with Deuteronomy 8:3, the lesson of the manna. Where Israel grumbled for food, the Son trusts His Father's word, passing the test Exodus 16:4 describes.

Jesus teaches His disciples to pray 'Give us each day our daily bread.' The prayer carries the pattern of the manna into everyday life: provision asked for and received one day at a time from the Father.

Jesus takes up Exodus 16 directly. The true bread from heaven is not the manna Moses gave but the bread the Father gives, and Jesus declares, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger.' The chapter's gift becomes a sign pointing to Him.

The crowd grumbles about Jesus as their fathers grumbled in the desert. Jesus contrasts the manna, which did not keep their fathers from death, with Himself, the living bread whose flesh is given for the life of the world. The wilderness story is replayed and surpassed.

A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, and whoever enters it rests from his own work as God did. The first Sabbath of Exodus 16:23-30, where Israel rested on bread already given, points toward the rest believers enter by faith.

The risen Christ promises the one who overcomes 'the hidden manna.' The manna once kept in a jar before the Testimony, Exodus 16:33-34, becomes a picture of the eternal provision God keeps in His presence for His faithful people.

study.oneStory:
In Eden God gave humanity every tree for food, Genesis 1:29 and 2:16, and bread came freely from His hand. After the fall, bread came by the sweat of the brow from a cursed ground, Genesis 3:19. Exodus 16 shows a people in the wilderness who can neither sow nor reap, and God feeding them again directly from heaven. It is a glimpse of the original generosity breaking into a fallen world, and it answers the question of whether the God who brought them out can keep them alive.

The chapter also answers the question of Egypt. Israel remembered Egypt as a place of full pots, but it was a place of slavery. The manna teaches a new way to live: not by the ration of a tyrant but by the daily gift of a Father, with a day of rest built in. It is a small picture of the life God intends for His people, freed from anxious labour and ordered by His word.

What the chapter sets up is the rest of Israel's story with God and bread. The Sabbath will be written into the covenant at Sinai. The Bread of the Presence will sit before the LORD in the tabernacle, Exodus 25:30. Israel in the land will be told not to forget the God who fed them with manna when their barns are full, Deuteronomy 8:10-18. And the prophets will hold out a future banquet for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6.

The story reaches its centre in Jesus, who feeds crowds in the wilderness, refuses to make bread for Himself in His temptation, and declares Himself the bread of life. At His table the church receives bread that proclaims His death, and believers pray each day for daily bread from the Father.

The story ends at a feast. Those who belong to Christ are promised the hidden manna, Revelation 2:17, and are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. In the new creation, 'Never again will they hunger,' Revelation 7:16, for the Lamb will shepherd them. The daily manna, gathered and gone by noon, gives way to a table that never empties.

sermon.title: Food in the Desert
sermon.why: Preached on Exodus 16:2-5, 27-35, Keller traces the manna's daily provision and the discipline of gathering only enough, drawing the line to Christ as the true bread from heaven who alone satisfies.

quiz.q: What did Israel complain about at the start of this chapter?

options.text: That they had no food and claimed they had eaten better as slaves in Egypt.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 record this exact complaint, longing for Egypt's pots of meat and bread.

options.text: That the water was too bitter to drink.
options.note: That complaint belongs to the previous chapter, at Marah, not this one about hunger.

options.text: That Moses had led them the wrong direction geographically.
options.note: Their complaint is specifically about food, not the route taken.

options.text: They made no complaint in this chapter.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 record a clear and bitter complaint about food.

quiz.q: How much manna was each person commanded to gather, according to verse 16?

options.text: An omer per person, exactly as much as was needed.
options.note: This fixed measure prevented both shortage and hoarding, as verse 18 confirms.

options.text: As much as each family could carry.
options.note: The command specified a fixed measure per person, not an open-ended amount.

options.text: Enough to last an entire week at once.
options.note: They were to gather daily, except on the sixth day when a double portion was allowed for the Sabbath.

options.text: No specific amount was commanded.
options.note: The omer measure was an explicit command.

quiz.q: What happened when some people kept manna overnight against instructions?

options.text: It became infested with maggots and began to smell.
options.note: Verse 20 describes this consequence of disobedience directly.

options.text: It multiplied into an even larger supply.
options.note: The opposite happened; the leftover manna spoiled rather than multiplying.

options.text: Nothing happened; the manna kept perfectly well.
options.note: The text explicitly says it spoiled, unlike the Sabbath-eve portion which stayed good.

options.text: The manna turned into quail.
options.note: The text describes spoilage with maggots, not a transformation into quail.

quiz.q: What made the manna gathered on the sixth day different from other days?

options.text: A double portion was gathered, and it did not spoil overnight, unlike other days.
options.note: Verses 22 to 24 describe this special provision for the Sabbath.

options.text: It tasted different from the manna on other days.
options.note: The text notes the amount and its preservation, not a change in taste.

options.text: No manna at all fell on the sixth day.
options.note: Manna did fall on the sixth day, in double portion; none fell on the seventh.

options.text: There was no difference; every day's manna behaved identically.
options.note: The sixth day's portion was uniquely preserved overnight without spoiling.

quiz.q: Why was a jar of manna kept before the Testimony, according to verses 32 to 34?

options.text: So future generations could see the bread the LORD gave Israel in the wilderness.
options.note: This is the explicit stated purpose, a lasting memorial for generations to come.

options.text: As food reserved for Moses' personal use.
options.note: The stated purpose is a memorial witness, not personal provision for Moses.

options.text: Because the manna in the jar was somehow more nutritious.
options.note: No such claim is made; its purpose was purely memorial.

options.text: No reason is given for keeping the jar.
options.note: Verse 32 explicitly states the memorial purpose.

questions: Israel grumbled that slavery in Egypt looked better than freedom with hardship. When has present difficulty tempted you to romanticize a past you were actually glad to escape?

God gave manna one day at a time, with no way to store it up for tomorrow except by disobedience. Where in your life are you trying to hoard security that God is asking you to trust Him for daily instead?

The Sabbath rest was tied directly to trusting God's provision, not just following a rule. What would it look like for you to rest this week not out of obligation but out of genuine trust that God will provide even when you stop working?
Jesus said He is the true bread from heaven, and whoever comes to Him will never hunger. What are you currently looking to for the kind of lasting satisfaction only Christ can actually give?

The jar of manna was kept so later generations would remember God's provision. What tangible reminder helps you remember God's past faithfulness when you are tempted to doubt His care in a new season?

translationNotes.note: What is it? renders the Hebrew phrase man hu, which many scholars believe is the origin of the name manna itself, a fitting name for a food Israel could not otherwise identify or explain.
The description white like coriander seed and tasting like wafers made with honey gives one of the Bible's most concrete sensory descriptions of a miraculous provision.

The closing note that an omer is a tenth of an ephah functions as an explanatory aside for readers unfamiliar with the measure, suggesting the text was compiled for an audience some distance from the original event.
